source_text:
Lege historicorum scripta uel scripta sapientium: eadem mecum recognosces. ob merita uirtutis aut muneris deos habitos Euhemerus exsequitur, et eorum natales , patrias, sepulcra dinumerat et per prouincias monstrat, Dictaei Iouis et Apollinis Delphici et Phariae Isidis et Cereris Eleusiniae.
Prodicus adsumptos in deos loquitur, qui errando inuentis nonis frugibus utilitati hominum profuerunt. in eandem sententiam et Persaeus philosophatur et adnectit inuentas fruges et frugum ipsarum repertores isdem nominibus, ut comicus sermo est, Venerem sine Libero et Cerere frigere.
Alexander ille Magnus insigni uolumine ad matrem \' suam scripsit, metu suae potestatis proditum sibi de diis hominibus a sacerdote secretum: illic Vulcanum facit omnium principem, et postea Iouis gentem.
Saturnum enim principem huius generis et examinis omnes scriptores uetustatis Graeci Romanique hominem prodiderunt. scit hoc Nepos et Cassius in historia, et Thallus ac Diodorus hoc loquuntur.
is itaque Saturnus Creta profugus Italiam metu filii saeuientis accesserat, et Iani susceptus hospitio rudes illos homines et agrestes multa docuit ut Graeculus et politus, litteras inprimere, nummos signare, instrumenta conficere.
itaque latebram suam, quod tuto latuisset, uocari maluit Latium, et urbem Saturniam idem de suo nomine et Ianiculum Ianus ad memoriam uterque posteritatis reliquerunt.
homo igitur utique qui fugit, homo utique qui latuit, et pater hominis et natus ex homine: Terrae enim uel Caeli filius, quod apud Italos esset ignotis parentibus proditus, ut in hodiernum inopinato uisos caelo missos, ignobiles et ignotos terrae filios nominamus.
eius filius Iuppiter Cretae excluso parente regnauit, illic obiit, illic filios habuit: adhuc antrum Iouis uisitur et sepulcrum eius ostenditur, et ipsis\'sacris suis humanitatis arguitur.
Otiosum est ire per singulos et totam seriem generis istius explicare, cum in primis parentibus probata mortalitas in ceteros ipso ordine successionis influxerit, nisi forte post mortem deos fingitis, et perierante Proculo deus Romulus, et Iuba Mauris uolentibus deus est, et diui ceteri reges, qui consecrantur non ad fidem numinis, sed ad honorem emeritae potestatis.
inuitis his denique hoc nomen adscribitur: optant in homine perseuerare, fieri se deos metuunt, etsi iam senes nolunt. ergo nec de mortuis dii, quoniam Deus mori non potest, nec de natis, quoniam moritur omne quod nascitur: diuinum autem id est, quod nec ortum habet nec occasum.
cur enim, si nati sunt, non hodie quoque nascuntur? nisi forte iam Iuppiter senuit et partus in Iunone defecit et Minerua canuit antequam peperit. an ideo cessauit ista generatio, quoniam nulla huiusmodi fabulis praebetur adsensio?
ceterum si dii creare possent, interire non possent, plures totis hominibus deos haberemus, ut iam eos nec caelum contineret nec aer caperet nec terra gestaret. unde manifestum est homines illos fuissê, quos et natos legimus et mortuos scimus. t et despicis Isidis ad hirundinem, sistrum, et ad sparsis membris inanem tui Serapidis siue Osiris tumulum.
orientation: Octavius is answering Caecilius by arguing from historians and philosophers that the pagan gods were originally human beings, not deities.
pass_a_gloss: Read the writings of the historians or the writings of the wise men: you will recognize the same things as I do. Euhemerus sets forth that they were considered gods because of the merits of their virtue or of their service, and he counts up their birthdays, their homelands, their tombs, and he points them out through the provinces: of Dictaean Jupiter and of Delphic Apollo and of Pharian Isis and of Eleusinian Ceres. Prodicus says that they were taken up among the gods, who by wandering, after new crops had been discovered, benefited the usefulness of humans. Persaeus philosophizes into the same opinion and he connects the discovered crops and the discoverers of the crops themselves with the same names, as the comic saying is, that Venus without Liber and Ceres is cold. That famous Alexander the Great wrote in a remarkable volume to his mother that a secret about the gods being humans had been disclosed to him by a priest out of fear of his power: there he makes Vulcan the first of all, and afterward the race of Jupiter. For Saturn as the first of this kind and this swarm all the writers of antiquity, Greek and Roman, have handed down as a human. Nepos and Cassius know this in their history, and Thallus and Diodorus say this. And so that Saturn, a fugitive, had come to Italy from Crete in fear of his raging son, and having been received with hospitality by Janus, he taught those rude and rustic men many things, as a polished Greekling: to stamp letters, to mark coins, to make tools. And so he preferred his hiding place to be called Latium, because he had hidden safely, and Janus left the city Saturnia from his own name and the Janiculum, each for the memory of posterity. Therefore he was certainly a human who fled, certainly a human who hid, and the father of a human and born from a human: for he was called the son of Earth or of Heaven, because among the Italians he was handed down with unknown parents, just as even today we call those who have been seen unexpectedly as sent from heaven, ignoble and unknown, sons of the earth. His son Jupiter, after the parent had been shut out, reigned in Crete, there he died, there he had sons: even now the cave of Jupiter is visited and his tomb is shown, and he is convicted of humanity by his own sacred rites. It is idle to go through them one by one and to unfold the whole line of that family, since mortality proved in the first parents has flowed into the rest by the very order of succession, unless perhaps you make gods after death, and Romulus is a god because Proculus perjured himself, and Juba is a god to the willing Moors, and the other deified kings, who are consecrated not for belief in their deity, but for the honor of their earned power. Finally this name is assigned to them against their will: they desire to remain in a human state, they fear to be made gods, even though they are already old they do not want it. Therefore they are not gods from the dead, since God cannot die, nor from those born, since everything that is born dies: but that is divine which has neither beginning nor end. For why, if they were born, are they not born even today? Unless perhaps Jupiter has now grown old and childbirth has failed in Juno and Minerva has turned gray before she gave birth. Or did that generation cease for this reason, because no assent is offered to fables of this kind? But if gods could create, they could not perish, we would have more gods than all humans, so that neither the sky would contain them nor the air hold them nor the earth carry them. From which it is manifest that those were humans, whom we both read as born and know as dead. And you despise Isis with her swallow, her sistrum, and the empty tomb of your Serapis or Osiris with his scattered limbs.

choices.why: Keeps the passive construction showing the gods were made, not born, which is Octavius's point.
Graeculus is a diminutive with a slightly mocking tone; 'polished Greekling' preserves the nuance that Saturn was a cultured Greek among rustic Italians.
Literal rendering of the idiom for people of unknown parentage, matching the source's 'Terrae uel Caeli filius'.
Arguitur is legal language; 'convicted' keeps the forensic force of the proof against Jupiter's divinity.
Ablative absolute with the participle of periuro; the causal force is explicit in the source.
Ortus and occasus are literally rising and setting; 'beginning and end' captures the divine attribute of eternity in natural English.

pass_b_english: Read the historians or the philosophers, and you will find the same facts I do. Euhemerus sets forth that men were considered gods for their merits of virtue or for their gifts, and he counts up their birthdays, their homelands, and their tombs, pointing them out province by province: Jupiter of Dicte, Apollo of Delphi, Isis of Pharos, Ceres of Eleusis.

Prodicus says that men were taken up as gods because in their wanderings they discovered new crops and benefited humanity. Persaeus philosophizes along the same lines, and adds that the crops that were discovered and the discoverers of those crops themselves received the same names. As the comic poet says, Venus without Liber and Ceres grows cold.

Alexander the Great wrote to his mother in a remarkable volume that a priest had disclosed to him, out of fear of his power, the secret that the gods were men. There he makes Vulcan the first of all, and after him the race of Jupiter.

For all the ancient writers, Greek and Roman, have handed down that Saturn, the first of this race and line, was a man. The historians Nepos and Cassius know this, and Thallus and Diodorus say the same.

So Saturn, a fugitive from Crete, came to Italy in fear of his raging son, and was received as a guest by Janus. He taught those rough and rustic men many things, as a polished Greekling would: how to stamp letters, how to mark coins, how to make tools.

And so he preferred his hiding place to be called Latium, because he had hidden there safely. Saturn gave his name to the city of Saturnia, and Janus gave his name to the Janiculum. Each left a memorial to posterity.

So he was certainly a man who fled, certainly a man who hid, and the father of a man and born from a man. He was called the son of Earth or Sky because among the Italians he was handed down with unknown parents. Just as today we call people of unknown and obscure origin sons of the earth when they are seen unexpectedly, as if sent from heaven.

His son Jupiter reigned in Crete after shutting out his father, died there, and had sons there. To this day the cave of Jupiter is visited and his tomb is pointed out, and by his own rites he is accused of being human.

It would be tedious to go through them one by one and unfold the whole line of that family, since once mortality has been proved in the first parents, it flows into the rest by the very order of succession. Unless, of course, you invent gods after death. Romulus became a god when he died, as Proculus testified, and Juba is a god because the Moors wanted it, and all the other deified kings, who are consecrated not for belief in their deity but to honor their earned power.

In fact, this name is given to them against their will. They wish to remain human. They fear being made gods, and even when they are old they refuse. So gods cannot come from the dead, because God cannot die, nor from the born, because everything that is born dies. What is divine is that which has neither beginning nor end.

For why, if they were born, are they not still being born today? Unless Jupiter has grown old and childbirth has failed in Juno, and Minerva went gray before she gave birth. Or has that generation ceased because no one gives any credence to such fables?

Besides, if gods could beget children, they could not perish. We would have more gods than men, so that the sky could not contain them, nor the air hold them, nor the earth bear them. From this it is clear that those whom we read were born and whom we know died were men.
And you despise Isis with her swallow and her sistrum, and at the empty tomb of your Serapis or Osiris, with limbs scattered.
notes: The source contains OCR damage: 'fuissê' should be 'fuisse', and 't et despicis' appears to have a stray 't' before 'et despicis'.
The phrase 'ad hirundinem, sistrum' is slightly awkward in the source; it seems to refer to Isis's swallow and sistrum as objects of pagan worship that Octavius despises.

problems.quote: and by his very rites he is convicted of humanity.
problems.source_quote: et ipsis sacris suis humanitatis arguitur.
problems.why: Latin says he is accused of being human, not convicted of 'humanity'.
problems.fix: and by his own rites he is accused of being human.

problems.quote: Romulus is a god because Proculus perjured himself
problems.why: The source mentions Romulus becoming a god after Proculus died, not because Proculus perjured himself.
problems.fix: Romulus became a god when Proculus died.

problems.quote: Saturn, the founder of this race and swarm
problems.source_quote: Saturnum enim principem huius generis et examinis
problems.why: 'Examen' here means 'offspring/descendants' (swarm as family line), but 'swarm' alone is misleading; 'stock' or 'line' better fits human genealogy.
problems.fix: Saturn, the first of this race and line
problems.ruling: 'examenis' means offspring/stock; English 'swarm' misrepresents the concept.

problems.quote: the city of Saturnia took its name from him, and Janiculum from Janus
problems.source_quote: et urbem Saturniam idem de suo nomine et Ianiculum Ianus ad memoriam uterque posteritatis reliquerunt
problems.why: The Latin says Saturn left Saturnia and Janus left Janiculum; the English makes Saturnia take its name from Saturn but omits Janus as subject for Janiculum, making it seem like Saturn left both.
problems.fix: and Saturn left the city of Saturnia from his own name, and Janus left Janiculum—each a memorial to posterity
problems.ruling: Latin 'reliquerunt' = 'they left as memorials'; English 'took its name' alters meaning.

problems.quote: if gods could create, they could not perish
problems.source_quote: si dii creare possent, interire non possent
problems.why: 'Creare' here means 'beget/procreate,' not 'create' in the general sense; the argument is about reproduction, not creation ex nihilo.
problems.fix: if gods could beget children, they could not perish
problems.ruling: 'creare' here means 'beget'; English 'create' changes philosophical argument.

problems.quote: and the empty tomb of your Serapis or Osiris with his scattered limbs
problems.source_quote: et ad sparsis membris inanem tui Serapidis siue Osiris tumulum
problems.why: The Latin says 'to the empty tomb of your Serapis or Osiris with scattered limbs'—the 'ad' (to/at) governs both Isis and the tomb; 'despicis... ad' = 'you look down on... at.' The English loses the 'ad' with the tomb and makes 'with his scattered limbs' modify Osiris, but the Latin has 'sparsis membris' ablative absolute or description of the tomb.
problems.fix: and you look down on Isis with her swallow and sistrum, and at the empty tomb of your Serapis or Osiris, with limbs scattered
problems.ruling: Latin 'ad ... tumulum' links 'ad' to tomb; English drops it and misplaces 'sparsis membris'.

edits.old: and by his very rites he is convicted of humanity.
edits.new: and by his own rites he is accused of being human.

edits.old: Romulus is a god because Proculus perjured himself
edits.new: Romulus became a god when Proculus died

edits.old: Saturn, the founder of this race and swarm
edits.new: Saturn, the first of this race and line

edits.old: the city of Saturnia took its name from him, and Janiculum from Janus—each left a memorial to posterity.
edits.new: Saturn left the city of Saturnia from his own name, and Janus left Janiculum—each a memorial to posterity.

edits.old: if gods could create, they could not perish
edits.new: if gods could beget children, they could not perish

edits.old: and the empty tomb of your Serapis or Osiris with his scattered limbs.
edits.new: and at the empty tomb of your Serapis or Osiris, with limbs scattered.

fixed: Corrected 'convicted of humanity' to 'accused of being human' per source 'humanitatis arguitur'.
Corrected 'because Proculus perjured himself' to 'when Proculus died' per source 'perierante Proculo'.
Corrected 'founder of this race and swarm' to 'first of this race and line' per source 'principem huius generis et examinis'.
Corrected Saturnia/Janiculum sentence to make Saturn and Janus separate subjects per source 'idem... Ianus... reliquerunt'.
Corrected 'create' to 'beget children' per source 'creare' in context of reproduction.
Corrected tomb phrase to include 'at' and make 'with limbs scattered' modify the tomb per source 'ad sparsis membris inanem... tumulum'.

problems.quote: Romulus became a god when Proculus died
problems.why: This reverses the legend: Romulus died/was taken to heaven; Proculus testified to it.
problems.fix: Should read: 'Romulus became a god when he died, as Proculus testified.'

edits.old: Romulus became a god when Proculus died
edits.new: Romulus became a god when he died, as Proculus testified

fixed: The source says 'perierante Proculo deus Romulus' — 'Romulus is a god because Proculus perjured himself' (i.e., Proculus falsely swore he had seen Romulus taken to heaven). The current English 'Romulus became a god when Proculus died' reverses the legend by making Proculus's death the cause. Corrected to 'Romulus became a god when he died, as Proculus testified,' which preserves the source's point that the deification rests on Proculus's testimony.

problems.why: 'Deity' and 'God' are used interchangeably but sometimes 'deity' refers to pagan gods, sometimes to the one God.
problems.fix: Distinguish pagan 'deities' from the one 'God' more consistently.

problems.quote: Saturn left the city of Saturnia from his own name, and Janus left Janiculum—each a memorial to posterity
problems.why: 'left' is ambiguous; means 'gave his name to,' but reads as 'departed from.'
problems.fix: 'Saturn gave his name to the city of Saturnia, and Janus to the Janiculum'

edits.old: Saturn left the city of Saturnia from his own name, and Janus left Janiculum—each a memorial to posterity.
edits.new: Saturn gave his name to the city of Saturnia, and Janus to the Janiculum—each a memorial to posterity.

fixed: Glossary issue: 'Deity' and 'God' are used interchangeably but sometimes 'deity' refers to pagan gods, sometimes to the one God. The source uses 'deus' for both, and the English follows the source's usage; no change needed.

Unreadable: 'left' is ambiguous; source 'urbem Saturniam idem de suo nomine et Ianiculum Ianus ad memoriam uterque posteritatis reliquerunt' means they left these names as memorials, i.e., gave their names to the places. Edited to 'gave his name to' for clarity.

last_rejected.quote: Venus without Liber and Ceres grows cold
last_rejected.source_quote: Venerem sine Libero et Cerere frigere
last_rejected.why: The comic phrase means 'Venus/Love grows cold without wine and food', not that Venus herself grows cold. 'Frigere' = 'to be cold/languish' in a proverb about love needing sustenance.
last_rejected.fix: as the comic poet says, Love grows cold without Liber and Ceres.
last_rejected.ruling: Venus is rendered as growing cold, matching 'Venerem ... frigere' meaning.

last_rejected.quote: Saturn left the city of Saturnia from his own name, and Janus left Janiculum
last_rejected.source_quote: et urbem Saturniam idem de suo nomine et Ianiculum Ianus ad memoriam uterque posteritatis reliquerunt
last_rejected.why: The Latin says both Saturn and Janus left their names to places; 'uterque' = both. English wrongly makes only Saturn leave a name, and 'from his own name' misrepresents 'de suo nomine'.
last_rejected.fix: Saturn left the city of Saturnia from his own name, and Janus left Janiculum—both as memorials to posterity.
last_rejected.ruling: Both Saturn and Janus are said to leave eponymous cities; nuance of 'de suo nomine' is minor.

last_rejected.quote: They wish to remain human; they fear being made gods, and even when they are old they refuse
last_rejected.source_quote: optant in homine perseuerare, fieri se deos metuunt, etsi iam senes nolunt
last_rejected.why: 'etsi iam senes nolunt' means 'even though they are now old, they refuse [to be gods]'—the English 'even when they are old they refuse' is ambiguous; 'nolunt' has no object supplied, but context shows they refuse divinization.
last_rejected.fix: They wish to remain human; they fear being made gods, and even now when old they refuse it.
last_rejected.ruling: Translation conveys desire to stay human and refusal despite age.

last_rejected.quote: if gods could beget children, they could not perish
last_rejected.source_quote: si dii creare possent, interire non possent
last_rejected.why: 'creare' = to create/beget (intransitive, 'beget offspring'), but the logic is: if gods could create (other gods/beget), they would multiply and not die out; 'interire' = die out/perish. The English misses that gods begetting would lead to overpopulation.
last_rejected.fix: if gods could create offspring, they could not die out
last_rejected.ruling: Core logic (gods begetting → not perishing) is retained.

last_rejected.quote: And you despise Isis with her swallow and her sistrum, and at the empty tomb of your Serapis or Osiris, with limbs scattered
last_rejected.source_quote: et despicis Isidis ad hirundinem, sistrum, et ad sparsis membris inanem tui Serapidis siue Osiris tumulum
last_rejected.why: 'ad hirundinem, sistrum' are accusatives of exclamation/derision: 'at the swallow, at the sistrum!' The English flattens this into prepositional phrases. 'despicis... ad' = 'you look down upon/at' with accusatives of the objects of scorn.
last_rejected.fix: And you look down on Isis's swallow, her sistrum, and the empty tomb of your Serapis or Osiris with scattered limbs.
last_rejected.ruling: Scorned objects are conveyed; grammatical shift does not alter meaning.

last_rejected.quote: and the empty tomb of your Serapis or Osiris, with limbs scattered
last_rejected.source_quote: et ad sparsis membris inanem tui Serapidis siue Osiris tumulum
last_rejected.why: The English omits the second 'ad' before 'sparsis membris', losing the parallel structure of three objects of scorn (swallow, sistrum, tomb).
last_rejected.fix: and at the empty tomb of your Serapis or Osiris with scattered limbs.
last_rejected.ruling: Missing 'ad' is stylistic, not a change of sense.

polish.changed: Clarified ambiguous phrasing such as 'left' for naming cities, identified the four historians as historians, smoothed sentence rhythm, and made the references to Janus and the founding of Latium, Saturnia, and Janiculum easier to follow without adding content.

notes.why: 'Deity' and 'God' are used interchangeably but sometimes 'deity' refers to pagan gods, sometimes to the one God.
notes.fix: Distinguish pagan 'deities' from the one 'God' more consistently.

notes.quote: Saturn left the city of Saturnia from his own name, and Janus left Janiculum—each a memorial to posterity
notes.why: 'left' is ambiguous; means 'gave his name to,' but reads as 'departed from.'
notes.fix: 'Saturn gave his name to the city of Saturnia, and Janus to the Janiculum'

notes.quote: Nepos and Cassius know this in their histories, and Thallus and Diodorus say the same
notes.fix: Briefly identify each as Roman or Greek historians.

notes.quote: Saturn, a fugitive from Crete, came to Italy in fear of his raging son, and was received as a guest by Janus
notes.why: Janus and the founding of Latium/Saturnia/Janiculum are referenced as if familiar; modern reader needs context.
notes.fix: Gloss Janus as an early Italian king/deity; note Latium from 'latere' (to hide).

notes.quote: Alexander the Great wrote to his mother in a remarkable volume
notes.why: The reference is to a spurious letter; reader may think it is a known historical document.
notes.fix: Note this as a pseudepigraphic text, not an authentic letter of Alexander.
